 LAS VEGAS (KSNV) — Two years after “no tax on tips” became a campaign promise, Las Vegas workers describe different experiences with the tax break: a refund for some, limits that leave others out, and concerns about how far the savings go.
 With Election Day approaching, the Culinary Union is pushing for changes to the deduction, arguing that it falls short for workers who receive mandatory gratuities and married couples who both earn tips.
 But he said his tips are down about 20% from the previous year, leaving less money for retirement savings or a vacation.
 For Jennifer Hanson, a banquet server at Red Rock, the benefit does not reach her banquet income.
 “So in theory, it sounds great, but it needs to be fixed,” Hanson said.
 The distinction depends on how the money is paid. According to the IRS, mandatory service charges distributed to employees are treated as wages rather than qualified tips. Voluntary tips can qualify for the deduction, including those received by eligible banquet workers.
 The law allows eligible workers to deduct up to $25,000 in qualified tips annually from their federal taxable income for tax years 2025 through 2028. The deduction begins phasing out for taxpayers with modified adjusted gross income above $150,000, or $300,000 for married couples filing jointly.
 It is a deduction, not a $25,000 refund or tax credit. Social Security and Medicare taxes still apply.
 Culinary Union Secretary-Treasurer Ted Pappageorge said the exclusion of automatic gratuities, including those paid in banquet settings, is among the union’s concerns. He also criticized the temporary nature of the relief.
 Another issue is the limit for married couples. Spouses who both earn qualified tips and file jointly share the $25,000 maximum deduction, rather than each receiving a separate limit. Married taxpayers must file jointly to claim the benefit.
 Pappageorge said the union has petitioned the Treasury Department and IRS and plans to continue pushing for changes after the election.
 For Hanson, the debate over tax relief comes alongside the weekly challenge of finding enough work.
 She said she now juggles seven to eight jobs, picking up on-call shifts at properties across the Las Vegas Valley after losing her full-time position.
 “It’s difficult to find work, and to get those coveted banquet jobs at all these different places is very difficult,” Hanson said. “It’s stress every single week, knowing what I will be working next week.”
 Hanson said tips help her cover basic expenses, including food, rent, and her car payment. While she wants changes to the tax rules, she also wants the stability of a single full-time job.
 “So I would love to have my full-time position back, have one job,” she said. “Like the American Dream isn’t nine jobs; it’s one.”
